name: Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior Detection
description: Methods and empirical studies for detecting coordinated link-sharing and inauthentic network behavior on social platforms, including the CooRnet/CLSB methodology, the VERA-AI Alert monitoring system, and investigations of deceptive information operations such as gambling promotion and 'zombie' networks. This is the researcher's longest-running and currently most active methodological line, central to the vera.ai WP4 leadership and ongoing 2025-2026 publications.

name: Platform Governance and Researcher Data Access
description: Work on how social media platforms regulate, restrict, or structure third-party research access to data—spanning the Digital Services Act researcher access provisions, EU Article 40(12) expert service with the JRC/ECAT, the state of social media research APIs post-CrowdTangle, and analyses of dataset thresholds (e.g., Meta's URL Shares Dataset). Reflects the agenda's current regulatory and institutional engagement.

name: Information Disorder and Disinformation Narratives
description: Theoretical and empirical work on misleading information in hybrid media systems, including the taxonomy of 'fake news', trust and post-truth publics (Ciarlatani), and the PROMPT project's monitoring of disinformation narratives around war, elections, and LGBTQI+ issues. A foundational and continuously updated thematic pillar of the researcher's programme.

name: Italian Election Studies
description: The MINE programme's core empirical line mapping Italian news media and social media dynamics around national elections, from the 2018 and 2019 campaigns through the 2022 general election, including partisan attention, hyperpartisan networks, and political parallelism analyses.

name: Facebook Algorithmic Governance and Visibility
description: Studies examining how Facebook's algorithmic curation, political content reduction policies, and platform design choices shape news visibility, partisan alignment, and user exposure—including the 2025-2026 analyses of Meta's political content policy and its effect on Italian parliamentarians' visibility, cited in EU parliamentary questions and national media.

name: Generative AI for Content Analysis and Research Methods
description: Methodological research on applying large language models and generative AI to communication research tasks—validating LLMs-in-the-loop pipelines, comparing embedding models for clustering political news, and studying AI-generated persuasive content—paired with the newly launched 'IA Generativa e Media' course, marking a growing and current methodological focus.

name: Health Misinformation Networks
description: Research mapping coordinated networks that circulate problematic health information, including COVID-19 fact-checking acceleration (MINE-FACTS) and cross-country studies in India and Nigeria funded by the Gates Foundation, examining how low-quality and ethnically/religiously inflected health content spreads via coordinated sharing.

name: Comparative International Election Studies
description: Cross-national analyses of coordinated behavior, political advertising, and partisan dynamics in non-Italian election contexts, including the 2021 German federal election, Brazilian post-Bolsonaro digital battlegrounds, and broader Latin American polarization studies—extending the researcher's coordinated-behavior methodology beyond Italy.

name: Political Polarization and Media Ecosystems
description: Conceptual and empirical work on how social and traditional media interplay to shape political polarization, insularity, and affective partisan engagement, including partisan community dynamics on Facebook and the broader theorization of polarization as a key concept in digital media research.

name: Platforms, Audiences, and Online Communities
description: Empirical and reflective studies of how platform affordances, cultures, and audience practices shape online sociality, identity, and community formation across sites like Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, Twitter/Mastodon, and LiveJournal.

name: Critical Analysis of AI Industry Imaginaries and Discourse
description: Studies examining how AI industry actors, media, and communities construct and circulate narratives, imaginaries, and framings (e.g., longtermism, techno-hagiography, 'quiet futuring', political-economy 'decoys') that shape public understanding and obscure or legitimize the underlying power structures of AI development.

name: Reflections on the State of Misinformation and Online Harm Research
description: Papers that step back from primary empirical study to critically assess the misinformation/online-harms research field itself — diagnosing biases (e.g., WEIRD-centrism, overreliance on cognitive proxies), mapping gaps in evidence (causal, longitudinal, cross-national), and proposing directions or borrowed lessons (e.g., from climate psychology) to make the field more rigorous and generalizable.

name: Theorizing AI's Social Role: Agency, Trust, and Public Perception
description: Papers that apply or extend social theory and communication-trust frameworks to understand the societal position of AI systems, ranging from conceptual demarcations of machine agency and formal multi-agent social frameworks to models of public trust in generative AI and empirical survey data on public attitudes toward AI adoption.

name: Computational Studies of Political Media and Advertising
description: Papers using large-scale computational or quasi-experimental methods to study political advertising, media capture, and ideological signaling on digital platforms, including causal analysis of ad effects, detection of covert advertiser influence on news coverage, and latent ideology estimation of political video content.

name: Survey Measurement Validity and Comparability
description: Papers examining methodological challenges in survey-based measurement, including whether respondents understand survey questions as intended, how online sample composition and quality checks affect representativeness and response validity, and how question wording and dataset differences affect cross-national and longitudinal comparability of trust measures.
